results.title: List price: CoreWeave's CFO says contract prices rose 25% in July | SecondSource
highlights:
# CoreWeave's CFO says contract prices rose 25% in July

How tight GPU compute is shows up in contract prices; public list-price indexes can't read it. CoreWeave, a cloud provider that specializes in renting out GPUs, had its CFO say on the August 11 earnings call that prices rose about 25% across all models in July. getdeploying, a public index that compiles list prices from dozens of providers' websites, showed only a 5% rise over the year at the time. A one-time price increase and a full-year cumulative rise cover different periods, and the two numbers don't measure the same kind of price.

CoreWeave's second-quarter report shows 98% of revenue came from committed contracts that are paid whether used or not, with pay-as-you-go at only about 2%. CoreWeave's website price for H100, US$6.16 per GPU-hour, is exactly the price the index picks up. The 25% most likely landed on newly signed and renewed contracts; that is the deep dive's reading from the quarterly report and the website, and the CFO didn't say which price it applied to. After other providers raised list prices in October, the index's one-year rise climbed to 18%.

results.title: Top Investor: CoreWeave Locked In Compute “Way, Way Under Market.” Rising GPU Prices Won’t Save It | TIKR.com
results.author: Gian Estrada
highlights:
27 after CoreWeave brought new capacity online at its first data center in Denmark, and fellow neocloud Nebius Group (NBIS) rose 11.22%.

...

The odd part is that GPUs have rarely been harder to rent. As Gavin Baker, managing partner and CIO of Atreides Management, said on TBPN on Oct. 27:

“October has kind of been a strange month because the price to rent, essentially any kind of a GPU, has gone up every day.”

...

Fixed prices cut both ways. If new supply pushes rents back down, those long contracts will protect CoreWeave’s revenue.

CoreWeave is adjusting, too. It raised prices about 25% across its GPU lineup in July, and management says contracts signed in the second quarter carry contribution margins 5 to 10 points above recent ones. Baker added that “CoreWeave is very aware of this. They’re trying to get more spot exposure.” Not all of its money is expensive, either: a Meta-backed $8.5 billion loan in March priced at about 5.9% fixed.

But higher prices only apply to new capacity, which costs “a truly vast amount” to build and must be financed in today’s market. Baker hopes the crunch concentrates supply in “the competent operators where they can finance it through prepayments.” That describes Nebius better: about 70% of its second-quarter deals came with prepayments covering 50% to 60% of the capex tied to them.

The September investor presentation gives evidence on both sides of that choice. It describes an A100 customer, a chip launched in 2020, renewing into 2029. It describes an H200 customer renewing for three years at a premium to its original contract. Those are two contracts, not a fleet. SAVRN’s price tracker adds a public check: tracked GPU list prices rose 6.1% on a same-item basis from September 11 to October 27, 2026 (chapter 8).

...

CoreWeave’s remaining performance obligations were $103.7 billion at June 30, 2026. Add about $0.5 billion of other expected revenue and the revenue backlog is $104.2 billion. That is about 22 times the $4,653 million of revenue it recognized in the first half of 2026 (SAVRN calculation).

The backlog rests on a handful of buyers. Three customers made up 36%, 26% and 10% of second-quarter revenue. Two of them each held 32% of receivables at June 30. The filings name the large contracts but not which letter belongs to which buyer.

The named contracts are large. OpenAI committed up to about $22.4 billion across three agreements running to May 31, 2031. Meta committed about $21 billion through December 20, 2032. NVIDIA signed a $6.3 billion order to buy any capacity CoreWeave cannot sell, through April 13, 2032. Jane Street committed about $6 billion in April 2026. Anthropic signed a multi-year agreement in April 2026 with no value disclosed.

Concentration has fallen but not gone away. Microsoft was 62% of revenue in 2024 and about 67% in 2025. In the second quarter of 2025 the top customer was 71% of revenue. A year later the top customer was 36%.

...

### List prices above the median, contracts far above the rent.

CoreWeave publishes on-demand prices on its website. SAVRN’s price tracker reads them every day. An NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 instance lists at $42.00 an hour for four GPUs, $10.50 per GPU-hour. An HGX B200 server lists at $68.80 an hour for eight GPUs, $8.60 per GPU-hour. HGX H200 lists at $6.31 and HGX H100 at $6.16. None of these prices changed between September 10 and October 26, 2026.

Against the market those prices sit high on older chips and low on the newest. CoreWeave’s HGX H100 is 1.50 times the median of 31 tracked on-demand H100 offers ($4.09). Its H200 is 1.17 times the median of 17 ($5.40). Its B200 is 1.02 times the median of 15 ($8.44). Its GB200 is 0.66 times the median of five tracked GB200 offers ($16.00). These are SAVRN Index figures and SAVRN calculations.

List prices are not what most customers pay. Committed contracts made up 98% of revenue in the second quarter, and the pricing page offers up to 60% off on-demand rates for committed use. The better guide is what CoreWeave says about its contracts. Its September investor presentation reports a price increase of about 25% across SKUs in July 2026. It reports short contracts of three to six months signed in the third quarter at about $40 million per MW of annualized revenue. That is about $3,333 per kW-month (SAVRN calculation: $40 million / 1,000 kW / 12).

results.title: CoreWeave Has To Charge More. Its Customers Have More Places To Spend.
results.author: Jennifer Evans
highlights:
CoreWeave’s own pricing has been moving upward. In September, the company said it was contracting new capacity at higher prices, including three-to-six-month agreements priced at approximately $40 million per megawatt on an annualized revenue basis. That is evidence of pricing strength in those agreements. It does not establish the economics of the entire fleet or the durability of those prices over several years. (investors. coreweave.com)

A provider’s need to charge more and its ability to secure higher prices can coexist. The test is whether enough customers will continue buying enough capacity at those prices to support the investment. We cannot establish from the announcement alone how much of the increase reflects scarcity, improved service, higher costs or the mix of contracts being signed.

results.title: CoreWeave CEO addresses "volatility in the capital markets" as company posts $3.66bn in revenue - DCD
results.author: Georgia Butler
highlights:
Current pricing per megawatt varies, with contracts of four-to-five years varying between 20-25MW, and those shorter contracts reaching up to $40m per megawatt. Additionally, older-generation GPUs are being priced at a premium due to strong demand, with Ampere and Hopper generations increasing between 30 and 50 percent quarter over quarter.

Intrator added that more than 130,000 GPUs come off contract in 2027, as do another approximately 170,000 GPUs in 2028. "We already have a robust pipeline of customers competing for this capacity," he said.
